title: Email Privacy & Encryption Security Checklist
metaDescription: Complete checklist to secure your email with encryption, private providers, and tracking protection. Protect sensitive communications step-by-step.
intro: Your emails contain sensitive information that companies and hackers want to access. This checklist helps you secure your communications with encrypted email providers, tracking protection, and privacy-focused practices that keep your messages truly private.

items.task: Switch to an encrypted email provider like ProtonMail or Tutanota
items.why: Gmail and other mainstream providers scan your emails for advertising and lack end-to-end encryption by default.
items.howTo: Sign up for ProtonMail or Tutanota. Start with the free plan to test features. Both offer end-to-end encryption and are based in privacy-friendly jurisdictions.

items.task: Confirm your provider uses zero-access encryption
items.why: Zero-access means even the email provider cannot read your messages, ensuring maximum privacy.
items.howTo: Check your provider's security page. Look for terms like 'zero-access' or 'zero-knowledge.' ProtonMail and Tutanota both implement this by default.

items.task: Enable two-factor authentication on your email account
items.why: 2FA prevents unauthorized access even if someone steals your password.
items.howTo: Go to account security settings. Enable 2FA using an authenticator app like Authy or Google Authenticator. Avoid SMS-based 2FA when possible.

items.task: Verify your email provider's legal jurisdiction
items.why: Providers in privacy-friendly countries face fewer data retention requirements and government surveillance demands.
items.howTo: Check where your provider is headquartered. Switzerland (ProtonMail) and Germany (Tutanota) have strong privacy laws. Avoid providers in Five Eyes countries when possible.

items.task: Review the provider's logging and data retention policies
items.why: Even private providers may log IP addresses or metadata that could identify you.
items.howTo: Read the privacy policy and transparency report. Look for minimal logging policies and automatic data deletion. ProtonMail logs minimal metadata; Tutanota logs even less.

items.task: Use end-to-end encryption for sensitive emails
items.why: E2E encryption ensures only you and the recipient can read messages, protecting against interception.
items.howTo: With ProtonMail, encryption is automatic between ProtonMail users. For external recipients, use password-protected emails or ask them to join an encrypted provider.

items.task: Verify recipient public keys for important communications
items.why: Key verification prevents man-in-the-middle attacks and ensures you're communicating with the right person.
items.howTo: In your encrypted email client, check the recipient's public key fingerprint. Verify it through a separate secure channel like Signal or in person.

items.task: Avoid sensitive information in subject lines
items.why: Subject lines are often not encrypted and can be seen by email servers and network administrators.
items.howTo: Keep subject lines generic like 'Meeting Update' or 'Document Review.' Put sensitive details in the encrypted message body instead.

items.task: Set expiration dates for sensitive emails
items.why: Auto-expiring messages reduce the risk of old sensitive information being compromised later.
items.howTo: In ProtonMail, click the clock icon when composing. Set expiration from 1 hour to 4 weeks. Tutanota offers similar features in their secure external email option.

items.task: Disable automatic image loading in emails
items.why: Email tracking pixels hidden in images can track when and where you open emails.
items.howTo: In email settings, turn off 'Load remote content automatically.' Most private providers block this by default, but verify your settings.

items.task: Use plain text emails for maximum privacy
items.why: HTML emails can contain tracking elements and are more complex, potentially hiding privacy threats.
items.howTo: In compose settings, choose 'Plain Text' instead of 'Rich Text' or HTML. Plain text is also more universally compatible and loads faster.

items.task: Set up email aliases for different purposes
items.why: Aliases protect your main email address and help you track which services sell or leak your information.
items.howTo: Create aliases like shopping@, work@, social@ using your provider's alias feature. ProtonMail Plus allows 5 aliases; consider services like SimpleLogin for unlimited aliases.

items.task: Use disposable email addresses for one-time signups
items.why: Burner emails prevent spam and protect your main address from being sold to marketers.
items.howTo: Use services like TempMail or Guerrilla Mail for one-time verifications. For longer-term use, create dedicated aliases you can disable later.

items.task: Access email through Tor or VPN when needed
items.why: Tor and VPNs hide your IP address and location from email providers and network observers.
items.howTo: Use Incognito Browser with built-in Tor for accessing email privately. ProtonMail has a .onion address for Tor users. Always use HTTPS connections.

items.task: Keep personal and work emails completely separate
items.why: Separation prevents cross-contamination of data and reduces the impact if one account is compromised.
items.howTo: Use different email providers if possible, or at minimum different accounts. Never forward between them or access both from the same device if handling sensitive information.

items.task: Regularly clean up old emails and accounts
items.why: Old emails can contain outdated sensitive information, and unused accounts become security liabilities.
items.howTo: Monthly, delete emails older than 1 year unless needed for legal/business reasons. Close unused email accounts and remove personal data before deletion.

items.task: Set up PGP encryption for contacts using other providers
items.why: PGP allows encrypted communication with anyone, regardless of their email provider.
items.howTo: Generate a PGP key pair using tools like GPG. Share your public key with contacts and request theirs. Many email clients like Thunderbird support PGP integration.

items.task: Verify your domain has proper SPF, DKIM, and DMARC records
items.why: These protocols prevent email spoofing and ensure your emails are delivered and trusted.
items.howTo: If using a custom domain, check DNS records for SPF, DKIM, and DMARC. Use tools like MXToolbox to verify configuration. Your email provider should guide setup.

items.task: Monitor your email addresses in breach databases
items.why: Knowing when your email is compromised helps you take immediate protective action.
items.howTo: Check HaveIBeenPwned regularly or set up breach notifications. If found in a breach, immediately change passwords and consider changing email addresses if severely compromised.

items.task: Use a secure email client with privacy features
items.why: Desktop clients often offer better security controls than web interfaces and work offline.
items.howTo: Consider Thunderbird with privacy extensions, or use your provider's official apps. Avoid Outlook and Apple Mail for sensitive communications due to limited privacy features.

items.task: Securely backup your encryption keys and recovery codes
items.why: Lost keys mean permanently lost access to encrypted emails, while insecure backups create vulnerabilities.
items.howTo: Export keys and recovery codes to encrypted storage like a password manager or encrypted USB drive. Store physical copies in a secure location like a safe.

pro_tips: Use Incognito Browser's Tor mode when accessing email accounts for maximum anonymity and to prevent browser-based tracking.
Create a unique, complex password for your email account and store it in a reputable password manager - never reuse this password elsewhere.
Consider using different email providers for different purposes: one for personal use, another for shopping, and a third for work communications.
Enable recipient verification in your encrypted email provider to ensure messages are only sent to verified contacts and prevent accidental data leaks.
Set up email forwarding rules to automatically organize messages by sender or keyword, helping you identify potential tracking or spam attempts.
